title: Neologism Learning for Controllability and Self-Verbalization
claim: A learned new token can be trained, then queried for its own natural-language meaning, then that meaning tested as a stand-in.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, divided by vertical rules, curved arrows showing training loop
description: A wide three-column figure with vertical divider lines and bold italic titles: Neologism Learning, Verbalization, and Plug-In evaluation. Each column uses the same example, a question about getting promoted. In the left panel, a prompt reading 'How do I get promoted? Give me a ~concept answer' has the neologism highlighted in pink. A curved arrow labeled 'steering' in red italics leads to a pink output box reading 'Excel visibly at your job, and then ask.' A return arrow labeled 'gradient signal' points back to the prompt. The middle panel asks 'What is a synonym for ~concept?' and an arrow leads to a pink box answering 'Here's a synonym: lack'. The right panel repeats the promotion prompt but substitutes the word 'lack' for the neologism, and an arrow leads to a pink output box reading 'Work hard. Be seen. Ask.' Pink highlights mark model-generated text and the neologism. The eye goes first to the titles, then to the pink boxes.
caption: At left: neologism learning places neologisms---new tokens---in natural language concepts, and trains them to predict concept-bearing outputs (e.g., "single-sentence answer"), while keeping the rest of the model fixed. Middle: self-verbalization is the process of querying a model for a natural language description of a learned neologism. Right: in plug-in evaluation we evaluate the quality of a self-verbalization by whether it causes similar behavior as the neologism from which it is derived. All text in this figure is demonstrative, not real model outputs.
abstract: Humans invent new words when there is a rising demand for a new useful concept (e.g., doomscrolling). We explore and validate a similar idea in our communication with LLMs: introducing new words to better understand and control the models, expanding on the recently introduced neologism learning. This method introduces a new word by adding a new word embedding and training with examples that exhibit the concept with no other changes in model parameters. We show that adding a new word allows for control of concepts such as flattery, incorrect answers, text length, as well as more complex concepts in AxBench. We discover that neologisms can also further our understanding of the model via self-verbalization: models can describe what each new word means to them in natural language, like explaining that a word that represents a concept of incorrect answers means ``a lack of complete, coherent, or meaningful answers...'' To validate self-verbalizations, we introduce plug-in evaluation: we insert the verbalization into the context of a model and measure whether it controls the target concept. In some self-verbalizations, we find machine-only synonyms: words that seem unrelated to humans but cause similar behavior in machines. Finally, we show how neologism learning can jointly learn multiple concepts in multiple words.
